speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DAMAGE IN THE UNITED KINGDOM, THE NETHERLANDS AND BELGIUM  MOTION OFFERING SYMPATHY AND HELP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you know, we have all been deeply moved by the news of the disasters both on sea and on land that have taken place as a result of the terrible storms raging about the United Kingdom, and the channel between the United Kingdom and continental Europe.
We do not know as yet just the extent of the disaster, but we do know that very many lives have been lost, that many, many families have been forced to evacuate their homes, and that there has been a great destruction of property. I think I can assume that I would have the consent of every hon. member if I were to put a motion at this time in connection with this disaster. We all remember what great comfort our people got out of the sympathy of the peoples of those lands when disasters overtook some of our fellow citizens in the Fraser valley, in Manitoba, in Rimouski and Cabano in my native province of Quebec. We all know how much good it does to people who are in the throes of such disaster to realize that they have the active and concrete sympathy of those they regard as their friends.
If I may have unanimous consent to move the motion, without the usual notice, I do move, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew):
That His Honour the Speaker be asked to convey to Her Majesty the Queen, to Her Majesty the Queen of the Netherlands and to His Majesty the King of the Belgians the deep sympathy of the Commons of Canada to the people of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Belgium who have been so sorely stricken by the appalling disaster which has befallen them and the earnest desire of the Canadian people to manifest their sympathy to the sufferers in such concrete form as, after more accurate information is available about the actual needs, will prove to be the most helpful to them in their great distress.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: DAMAGE IN THE UNITED KINGDOM, THE NETHERLANDS AND BELGIUM  MOTION OFFERING SYMPATHY AND HELP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be permitted to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in seconding the 68108-974
motion that has been placed before the house. I know all hon. members will regard this as an opportunity to express their own sympathy with those who are suffering so severely in Britain, in Holland and in Belgium at this time. As many hon. members will have heard in the news broadcast within the last hour, the floods are increasing on an even greater scale and those who have suffered so greatly already would appear to be facing even worse trials than those they faced before.
While the terms of suffering cannot be measured in the loss of life as given in numbers alone, nevertheless it must have impressed all hon. members who heard the latest reports that since this morning the figures have risen to 397 known dead in Britain, 464 in Holland and 27 in Belgium, with the accompanying statement that this probably represents only a part of what the loss will actually be.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has pointed out that at a time when we felt something of the damage and sorrow that can come from floods here in our own country we were greatly heartened by the evidence of sympathy that came to us from across the ocean. I happened to be in Winnipeg on the day when a large air transport arrived from Great Britain carrying goods and supplies which had been sent from there to assist the sufferers in that area. I know something of what the effect was on the minds of those who were suffering at that time and who realized that with the privations under which the people of Great Britain had been living they had gone to the extent they had in sending these things for their assistance.
We also received succour and assistance from the people of Holland and Belgium. I know that this cannot be reduced to the terms of a return for what was done, but nevertheless we know, from what they did, what our evidence of sympathy at this time may mean. I heard this latest report just before I came into the chamber and I did not have an opportunity to speak to the Prime Minister, but I would place before him the suggestion that with the extent of the disaster being as it is it might perhaps be desirable to consider the possibility of taking initial steps to set up a committee of some kind so that in every community something

Floods
may be under way, and when the type of assistance that is to be given can be determined by the governments of Great Britain, the Netherlands and Belgium it will then be possible to proceed with the utmost speed.
I think that that might be worth while, considering the encouragement that would come from the knowledge that positive action had been taken along that line. It might well be that a non-partisan committee under the chairmanship of Mr. Speaker could proceed to lay down general plans and indicate to mayors and reeves throughout Canada that preliminary arrangements might be undertaken to meet whatever situation does arise as a result of the decisions of these governments.
This storm and the floods accompanying it are stated to be the worst in 500 years and I do feel that our attitude in regard to it might well be measured by the extent of the tragedy which has visited the countries which have been named by the Prime Minister in this motion.

maintopic: DAMAGE IN THE UNITED KINGDOM, THE NETHERLANDS AND BELGIUM  MOTION OFFERING SYMPATHY AND HELP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this group would like to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in supporting the motion which has just been made. We appreciate the prompt action taken by the Prime Minister because we realize the many disturbing and perplexing problems that must come to his desk in these strenuous days. Yet he finds time to take this most humane and friendly action.
This motion this afternoon is just another indication of how small the western world is becoming. We think of extending aid to countries on the other side of the Atlantic as we would of extending aid to a neighbouring province or a nearby country. I am glad indeed that the Prime Minister mentioned material aid because after all that is what will be of the greatest assistance to the people concerned as soon as help of that kind can be properly measured and extended.

maintopic: DAMAGE IN THE UNITED KINGDOM, THE NETHERLANDS AND BELGIUM  MOTION OFFERING SYMPATHY AND HELP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have no hesitation in giving our unanimous support to the motion which has been moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). We think it is only right that we in Canada, who have been the recipients of assistance from the various countries that are now stricken, should do everything we can to help these people in return. Even if they had not helped us I am sure the Prime Minister would have brought forward a motion of this kind. In addition to sending our expressions of sympathy and all the moral support we can at this time, we feel that out of the blessings we have received
[Mr. Drew.)
from Providence we should be prepared to assist these people in a material way. We will back the Prime Minister and the government in whatever they want to do.

subtopic: GANDER AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal orally with these three questions. I have for some time been fully aware that terminal building facilities at the major airports operated by my department are inadequate to meet the rapidly growing needs of civil aviation. Many representations to this effect have been received both from the public generally and from commercial air lines. Concentration on the defence program has, however, meant that expansion of terminal facilities, along with many other desirable projects, has had to be deferred. I am glad to be able to report that I have instructed my officials to proceed as rapidly as possible with the preparation of the necessary architectural plans for expansion of airport terminal facilities so that construction may begin just as soon as funds can be made available.
We have already completed small new terminals at the lakehead and at Moncton during the past year. Blueprints for a new building at Saskatoon, made necessary by national defence use of buildings previously employed for civil purposes, are almost completed, and this building will be constructed during 1953. At Gander we are improving the interior of the existing terminal through the provision of Canadian films and the installation of Canadian literature, exhibits, maps and murals. In addition, the preparation of blueprints for expansion of the Gander terminal facilities is now under way, and it is expected that these plans will be ready in time to allow construction to begin later this year.
My officials are also studying how best the present facilities can be expanded at Malton, and I have asked that plans be ready by the end of 1953 or early in 1954, if possible, so that if funds can be made available a contract for the expansion can be let promptly. At Dorval we are fully aware of

Questions
the need for a major change to combine both iomestic and international terminal facilities in a much enlarged terminal building. I have directed my officials to reach an early decision as to whether a completely new terminal should be constructed in a new location or whether the existing domestic terminal can be used as the core of a new terminal. As soon as this decision has been reached, instructions will be issued for the preparation of plans and specifications.
In addition, my officials are well advanced with the preparation of specifications for a new terminal building of a size and type which would be suitable for use either in Ottawa or in Winnipeg. New buildings are required and will be provided in both places as funds become available. It is my hope to see construction initiated over the next two or three years for the necessary new terminal facilities at all our major airports to keep abreast of the growth of civil aviation.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question which I had intended to ask the Secretary of State for

External Affairs but as he is not here I should like to direct it to the Prime Minister. Was the Canadian government informed or consulted as to changes in United States foreign policy with respect to Formosa, as stated by President Eisenhower in his speech at noon today? Will the minister make a statement on what stand the government took, or what stand it now takes on this important question, which it is considered in many quarters might have serious consequences for the peace of the world?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FORMOSA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
In the absence of the Secretary
of State for External Affairs, and anticipating that such a question might be asked from some quarter of the house, I got a note from the officials of the department.
It will be appreciated that the government have not had an opportunity to study the text of President Eisenhower's announcement regarding the modification of the order to the seventh fleet, as this announcement was made only about an hour ago. I may say, however, that the presidential order to the seventh fleet, issued on June 27, 1950, was made on the sole responsibility of the United States government. The modification of the order announced today by President Eisenhower is also made on the sole responsibility of the United States government. Late Friday last, the Canadian embassy was informed about the forthcoming statement to be made by President Eisenhower, but it was not suggested that we should express our views about it. The Canadian ambassador, Mr. Wrong, arrived in Ottawa this morning. He is here on a visit which had been arranged before this incident occurred. Advantage will be taken of his presence to discuss this matter and its background more fully.

subtopic: FORMOSA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: I would ask that we might have a statement at an early date with respect to another and, in my opinion, a much more important point raised in the speech by President Eisenhower today. That is his statement that the United States government is no longer going to regard itself as bound by any secret treaties with nations which have not observed their part of such undertakings. It is not necessary to point out what those treaties are. We all know what they are. It would seem to me that the consequences of that action are so far-reaching that we should have a statement in the house at the earliest possible date as to what this means in terms of Canadian policy with relation to the same subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: FORMOSA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
I feel quite satisfied that there are no secret undertakings with Canada
Inquiries oj the Ministry that will be affected by the policy announced by President Eisenhower. The whole matter will be given careful consideration because, though they may be matters of entirely domestic concern to the people of the United States, all of us are so close together that what is of domestic concern to any one of us is apt to have the kind of repercussions upon the fate of others that makes it very desirable for us to give most definitive consideration to those matters.

subtopic: FORMOSA
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT AS TO CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext: Without extending the discussion I wish to indicate the point I had in mind. The statement by President Eisenhower does not relate to secret undertakings with other nations. It obviously referred to those secret agreements out of which grow certain divisions of authority which today have a very profound effect on the whole world situation. It is in relation to these matters, and particularly as they relate to Europe, on which I would hope we would have a definite statement as soon as possible. [Later:]

the second reading of Bill 'Jo. 103, to amend the National Defence Act.
He said:	The government has, as might
well have been expected, Mr. Speaker, given careful consideration to the various points raised in the debate on the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill. The Leader if the Opposition (Mr. Drew), and several >ther hon. members, argued that if an emergency existed that justified the present emergency powers legislation, it was not necessary to have any amendment to the National Defence Act since the power already existed to appoint one or more associate ministers of national defence during an emergency and for six months thereafter.
It seems to me that hon. members who advanced' that argument did not take into account the distinction between the international emergency that parliament declared did exist when it enacted the emergency powers legislation and the emergency defined n the National Defence Act and contemplated in the War Measures Act. The Emergency Powers Act states categorically that an international emergency exists which threatens the security of Canada, and that certain emergency powers might, therefore, be required by the government. On the other hand, the National Defence Act, in section 20, defines emergency as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) pointed out during the course of his argument, as war, invasion, riot or insurrection, real or

apprehended. One finds the same definition in the War Measures Act, which empowers the governor in council to exercise the powers conferred upon him only when the governor in council has taken the responsibility of declaring, by proclamation, that by reason of the existence of a real or apprehended war, invasion or insurrection, such measures are required.
We do feel that the present conditions are not normal conditions. We do agree with the hon. members that, in fact, war is being waged in Korea. We do agree that if war were not being waged in Korea, a war which might have serious consequences for the free world at large, young Canadians would not be voluntarily offering up their services and risking their lives for something of the character of an ordinary police action. It was because there was a realization by the Canadian people that it was desirable, in the interests of freedom in the world, that a stand be taken in Korea that would make it apparent that aggression was not going to be allowed to pay. This has resulted in very serious, active, and unfortunately destructive warfare, which has cost many lives and the destruction of a great deal of property. I believe it is nevertheless fortunate for the world that the United Nations did have the resolute determination that they were going to demonstrate that aggression did not pay. If that had not been done, no one can be sure what the consequences might have been.
Fortunately, the consequences have not been the kind of war that the hon. gentleman's generation and mine have twice known in our lifetime. The government felt that the emergency contemplated by the War Measures Act, and the emergency contemplated by the National Defence Act, were the kind of emergencies that we had been through from 1914 to 1918 and from 1939 to 1945 and not this twilight period which cannot be said to be peace but is fortunately not world war. I, therefore, felt that if that twilight situation required something to be done now, that would have to be done too under the other kind of emergency, it would be proper to come to parliament and tell parliament what our intentions were and to get parliament to express its views on the propriety of the action being proposed.
Hon. gentlemen will also have noticed that when the Emergency Powers Act was framed it was circumscribed in many ways. We do not complain about that, and I think it was wisely circumscribed. It was provided that nothing in that Emergency Powers Act would apply in this twilight period that would affect the liberty of persons and that

there should be no expenditure of money that was not appropriated by parliament itself. Human nature is such that to provide for an associate minister of national defence there has to be some money provided as well to compensate for the services that the associate minister will be expected to render. It was felt, therefore, that there had to be parliamentary action before any decision of that kind could be implemented, and that as there had to be parliamentary action it would be proper to have that parliamentary action cover both the policy decision and the appropriation necessary to implement the policy.
I would hope, as I am sure the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) would hope, that there would be as few occasions as possible when the executive would have to dispense with the decision of parliament in any matter of importance, and that hon. gentlemen will not think it was wrong to come to parliament for this action if in fact the decision to be made and to be implemented is the right kind of decision.

speechtext:
National Defence Act
But the theoretical or ideal development of the forces of a country is always circumscribed by the financial and manpower resources of that country. We or the government have to decide what portion of the annual production of the country it is desirable to set aside for defence purposes in any given year. That portion has to be the best kind of balance we can make between the defence requirements and the other requirements of the nation as a whole, and it necessarily varies according to the degree of danger for which the defence forces have to be ready. When a determination has been made as to what proportion of the gross national product of the nation it is proper for the nation to expend as an insurance policy for its safety and continued existence, that is the cloth that can be cut.
It was felt that it would be preferable to have one minister receiving the representations of the various services, co-ordinating them and determining between them what allocation could be made to each service. It would seem to us to be inevitable that if there were three ministers, one for each of these three services, each would naturally feel more keenly the importance of his service than that of the other services, and that there would be a competitive spirit. As honest, unprejudiced and unbiased as it would be possible for the head of one service to be and still be fair to his service, it seemed to us that he would naturally want as large a slice as he could get of the total amount appropriated for defence. It was felt that that competitive spirit had been the cause of duplication that was unnecessary and that it made for additional expense during the last war.
I remember many anxious moments during the discussions of the last war about the proper set-up of the hospital facilities for the services, and finding it difficult for me, a civilian, to appreciate that it was so necessary that there be no common hospital services for the treatment of the men of the three services. After all, they were Canadian men or Canadian women, serving the Canadian cause, and the health of each one was not so very different in character from the health of the other. But those who had military experience felt that it was necessary to retain the identity of these services, and that even in the hospital and medical branches the line of division had to be kept quite clear, distinct and apart.
Well, after the war, rightly or wrongly we decided that there would be a serious attempt to cut out some of the duplication, and not do it under the stress of fighting action going on at the same time, and we

placed the department under one minister and one civilian departmental set-up. And we have not yet had reason to backstep, or reason to admit that that was not a good policy.
We, therefore, when approaching this matter of providing additional responsibility and additional service for the Department of National Defence, thought that the best way was to retain the one over-all civilian set-up, with an associate minister rather than a separate minister. Under the bill proposed, this co-ordination of the services will be preserved. Both the minister and the associate minister of national defence will be charged with the apportionment of the available public money, men and military supplies among the three services.
As I said a minute ago, we do realize, and we did realize after the war, that under wartime conditions, which we did not want to interfere with during wartime, when there were almost three separate departments of national defence, under three ministers, there had been quite a good deal of duplication of the civilian services; and we expected that considerable saving of the taxpayers' money could be made by having this unified civilian structure of the armed services, thus assisting in the closer co-ordination of all three.
I am inclined to think that, if we set up an entirely separate department of national defence for air, with a separate minister and separate deputy minister, inevitably there would be developed once again all this amount of duplication and overlapping which it was our policy to eliminate to the extent to which it could be eliminated.
Now, perhaps what the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) meant was that we should have an associate minister of national defence who would have special responsibility for the Royal Canadian Air Force and its supporting services. Well, I would admit this, that the argument against that course is not as strong as the argument against an entirely separate department. But I do not think such an arrangement would go any greater distance towards meeting the objection raised by the hon. member that there was not a clear and precise division of functions between the minister and the associate minister.
If there is to be co-ordination-and everyone agrees that there should be-the minister would have to continue to have responsibility for that co-ordination, and therefore for overall policy in respect of the three services. The associate minister would, therefore, be limited in fact to the oversight and supervision of administration of the air force and

perhaps an indefinite fraction of the existing civilian side of the department which supports the three services.
It seems to me that this would not be a very tidy arrangement, and that it would not be very long before there would have to be an associate deputy minister for air, and that would immediately start a duplication of the civilian side, again, which we have endeavoured to eliminate.
I think that the field of activity of the associate minister would, under such an arrangement, be more restricted than what is contemplated by our proposal, under which proposal the associate minister will, in effect, have ordinary supervision over all the administrative activities which come under the deputy minister, for supply, for procurement, for accounting and auditing, and what might be described in general terms as the housekeeping activities of national defence.
That was what I was trying to indicate when I said on January 22, as reported at page 1240 of Hansard:
The associate minister, in addition to carrying on the work of the minister when the minister is away, will keep more closely in touch with matters of administration relating to the services. If I may repeat it is expected that the associate minister would act for and exercise the powers of the minister when the minister is away and deal with matters of administration relating to the three services, including requisitions for construction, equipment and supplies, submissions on similar matters to the governor in council and to the treasury board, control of the establishment, appointment and supervision of the civil employees and service personnel, approval of expenditures, orders, instructions and plans within the lines of agreed policy.
I doubt if it is possible to define the functions any more precisely and at the same time accomplish what the government really has in mind. We are not trying to divide up the department, or create something like two departments, or trying to create a department and a sub-department. What we are trying to do is to make it possible, as I said last Thursday, for responsibility to be shared between ministers. I believe, as I said then, that what is proposed will be satisfactory only if the minister and the associate minister work closely together in all matters, so that each will be really familiar, not with all the details, but with the general lines of the operation of the whole department, and of all three services.
This is really important, so that when, as so frequently happens, one minister has to be absent from Ottawa, the other will be sufficiently familiar with the whole department to act effectively in the whole field of its operations.
National Defence Act
I do not believe that an arrangement like this can work unless there is an exceptional degree of harmony between the minister and the associate minister, and an even greater degree of frankness and understanding than is necessary between two ministers of the government having quite separate departments. That was one reason why there was some hesitation before proposing sharing of the responsibility for this portfolio. As hon. members know, it is intended, if this legislation is approved, that the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney) shall become associate .minister.
For some time before he became a member of the government, the Solicitor General had been parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Defence. Their relationship had proved to be very satisfactory to themselves, to us and to the personnel of the department. As a result of that experience, both the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Solicitor General were convinced that they could make an arrangement like this one work. I may say to the house that when I first suggested it to the minister he welcomed its acceptance, and indicated to me that for some time he himself had been thinking of suggesting precisely the same arrangement.
What we are proposing is not a new departure. If hon. members will look up the legislation adopted in 1940, which was 4 George VI, chapter 21, they will see that in addition to providing for a minister of national defence for air and a minister of national defence for naval services the legislation provided also that the minister of national defence should have co-ordinating functions in respect of all three services and that there should be an associate minister of national defence who should act for the minister whenever he was absent from Ottawa and who at all times should be entitled to exercise the powers of the minister over the whole range of his responsibility unless the governor in council otherwise directed. The governor in council never otherwise directed.
The only hon. gentleman who ever occupied the post of associate minister of national defence is the present dean of the house. I am sure it is his view that the success of this kind of arrangement-and it was a success-did depend upon a very high degree of mutual confidence, mutual respect and harmony such as existed throughout all those war years between the associate minister and the minister of national defence with whom he was associated.

National Defence Act
What is more, I do believe that Canadians generally would agree that Canada was exceptionally well served by that partnership between the late regretted hon. gentleman who was minister of national defence and the associate minister, who fortunately is still with us in this House of Commons. Of course the parallel is not absolutely complete, as hon. gentlemen opposite will no doubt point out. The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) was also minister of national defence for air and that was his principal responsibility. But he did serve actively as associate minister. He was able to serve successfully in that capacity because he was at all times familiar, and kept himself at all times familiar, with the general trend of departmental activity in connection with the three services.
As hon. gentlemen will remember, there was also, in the person of the present premier of Nova Scotia, a minister of national defence for naval services. The minister of national defence for naval services under the act of 1940 could also exercise all the powers of the minister of national defence in his absence and in the absence of the associate minister of national defence. It did quite often happen that he had to exercise those powers.
During all that period I do not recall a single occasion on which anyone in this house suggested that there was any difficulty about establishing where ministerial responsibility lay for the administration of national defence. When any question arose in this house it seemed to me, and I think by the way it was acquiesced in by ail members of the house, that it was appropriate that the one of the three who did get up to answer the question should be dealing with the problem.
It is intended, if this legislation is approved, to vest in the associate minister precisely the same powers the associate minister enjoyed during the war years. The minister of course will have the immediate responsibility for defence policy. As all hon. members know, that is a responsibility which is shared constitutionally by all his colleagues and in a special degree, under our system, by the prime minister. Apart from the general constitutional responsibility, the responsibility for specific acts which require ministerial approval will of course rest with whichever minister gives that approval. In each case that will be a matter of record and the degree of responsibility would be precisely the same if there was no associate minister but merely an acting minister when the minister was absent.

I might say that the course which has been recommended to the house was proposed only after long and careful consideration of all the alternatives. We came to the conclusion that it was a course which it was hoped would achieve a realistic sharing of the heavy responsibilities for our defence services and the degree of ministerial control required for the very large operations which are involved.
I think hon. members will agree that it is appropriate that a fair trial should be made of any modification and will also share our hope that if there is a fair trial made of it it will prove to work as satisfactorily this time as we know it did in fact work through the co-operation, collaboration and mutual respect which the late minister of national defence and his associate minister had for each other during those other years of also very heavy responsibility.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposiiion):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment now before us is of much greater importance than might appear at first glance. What is proposed by this bill is that parliament enact a measure which will add another section to the National Defence Act. This would leave in its present form section 6 which permits the appointment of three additional ministers of national defence and would provide for the appointment of an associate minister of national defence without including in that section any definition of his authority.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in arguing against the suggestion that there be an associate minister of national defence for air, has contended that this might create confusion and division of authority. Yet, having said that, he has also made the statement that he does not recall a single occasion when any difficulty arose between the ministers who previously occupied the different positions under the measure passed in 1940. If under the stress of a world war it was possible for the ministers to carry out their responsibilities in respect of the different services without any difficulty in determining the boundaries of their authority, then it would seem that the Prime Minister has placed before us a most effective argument as to why there should now be an associate minister of national defence for air. He has assured us that in the experience of this government that could be done without creating any difficulty as to the measure of authority exercised by any single minister.
However, there is one aspect of the opinions placed before us by the Prime Minister which it seems overlooks the situation with which we are actually dealing.

The Prime Minister has said that the appointment of this minister will assist in the administration of the Department of National Defence. What has not been pointed out is that this subject has become one of immense importance to the members of the house because of the demonstrated fact that there has been a breakdown in the administration of the Department of National Defence. To appoint another minister with similar powers, no better defined than those already being exercised by the minister who occupies that office, will not solve the difficulties that have already been demonstrated to the members of the house.
The Prime Minister has said that there is a distinction between the emergency we now face and the emergency contemplated by section 6 of the National Defence Act which would permit the appointment by the government of three additional ministers of national defence. He points out that the National Defence Act defines the emergency which would be the basis for action under that act as war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended. The Prime Minister did go on to say that there is a real war in Korea. Consequently there is no question about the fact that in accordance with the words of the Prime Minister today the type of emergency contemplated by this act is in existence. If that is so, then the government could act under the present legislation if it saw fit to do so.
I agree that it would be desirable that such action should not be taken because the kind of emergency undoubtedly does not exist which should deny to us in this house a full opportunity to debate the authority that any minister will have. I submit that the only justification for emergency legislation of any kind is that the emergency is of a nature which requires a more expeditious procedure than would ordinarily be afforded by bringing legislative measures before the house and having them fully debated. I do not think that anyone will contend that there is not ample opportunity to discuss this legislation at this time. The very fact that the bill is brought before us demonstrates that there is time to discuss it. That being the case, I suggest that we should not only have the proposal for an additional minister but we should have the details as to what the authority and responsibility of that minister will be, to be incorporated in the measure before us, thus leaving no doubt as to what his responsibilities are going to be if he is appointed.
The fact that this subject is now before us in this way and that the Prime Minister
National Defence Act
has supported his presentation of the measure by arguments that it has worked well in the past should not divert from the mind of any hon. member in the house the fact that there is a situation with which we should be dealing and that this is the time to deal with that situation. The Prime Minister has said that we should have coordination of all activities related to national defence under a single minister. We should. Whatever is placed before us should make it possible for us to be able to assure ourselves that there is going to be effective co-ordination. That co-ordination has not existed, not only as between the department and the government but within the department itself. No single incident could better demonstrate the need for some effective change at this time in the whole operation of the Department of National Defence than the information which we have been given by the minister himself that not a single one of the 1,200 recommendations made by the auditors dealing with the methods of supervising the affairs of the department had reached 'the minister. If that is co-ordination, then it is certainly not the kind of co-ordination we want to perpetuate by a measure adopted by this house.
Granted that the minister might not have the time to read every recommendation that is made in detail or to communicate the effect of these recommendations to the department, but, Mr. Speaker, we are confronted with the admission that not one of these extremely important recommendations was read by the minister or communicated by him to the government. If that is the situation which we are going to perpetuate by the measure now before us, then I suggest that members of the house are not accepting their responsibility to the people of Canada and the members of the armed forces at this time. The words that are before us are clear enough. It has been demonstrated beyond question that there has been a breakdown of administration. It is not any single incident of that breakdown with which we are dealing. We are dealing with a breakdown of administration in the Department of National Defence for which the government as a whole is responsible.
Nothing less than new legislation which will deal with that breakdown is adequate to deal with the extremely serious situation before us. The situation will not be solved by appointing another minister to carry on the same unsatisfactory methods. That is exactly what we are being asked to support. The Prime Minister has said that he hopes we will deal with the merits of the proposal before us and not with procedure. The merits

National Defence Act
of the proposal before us rest on the adequacy of that proposal and not merely on the appointment of a minister. The merits of what is before us will be determined by the extent to which the measure before us does or does not deal with the breakdown which has been so abundantly demonstrated.
It is also clear from what has been placed before us that many of the difficulties which have been disclosed have been the result of a failure to define the responsibility of different officials within the department. We are asked to appoint a minister without defining his responsibilities. We are simply told that he will have the general responsibility of carrying on the system that already exists. What I should say is that he is to be appointed to carry on the complete lack of system that has been demonstrated. That is what we are really being asked to do. The Prime Minister has said that if there were an associate minister of national defence for air it would lead to a competitive interest on the part of that minister which would create confusion. If that argument is to be accepted, then how is it to be rationalized with the statement of the Prime Minister that he does not recall any case where that competitive spirit caused any difficulty when there was a minister of defence for air, a minister of defence for the navy, and in addition an associate minister with powers similar to those of the minister that the government now seeks to appoint?
The two statements do not go hand in hand. The fact is that, whatever details might be open to debate in regard to the general administration of the defence activities of this country during the war, it will be generally agreed that the Prime Minister was correct in saying that each of these ministers was able to deal with the particular responsibility he had, without any difficulty in defining what the measure of those responsibilities really was. That being so, we simply say:	Accept the statement of the
Prime Minister-that is the last statement- that there was no difficulty even under all the pressure of war in defining the limits of responsibility. Accept that statement and then appoint an associate minister of defence for air and define his responsibilities under the measure that this house will be called upon to adopt.
Now, we have been told that so complete was the breakdown of supervision that it will never be possible to tell what the losses were. I know that some attempt has been made to tell the members of this house in dollars and cents what the losses were. But we have the statement of one of the outstanding chartered accountants in Canada

to the effect that so confused and so ineffective was the system that it will never be possible to tell what was actually lost. What more can be placed before the members of this house to demonstrate the need of some new system than that statement by a man whose word should be accepted by all members of this house in that respect?
I am not arguing that any human being who is called upon to perform a service such as that which was performed in the consideration of certain limited aspects of the administration of the Department of National Defence should be regarded as infallible. Nevertheless, I would point out that whatever argument may be made about the interpretation to be placed on certain words, there has been a finding by an outstanding chartered accountant that the methods of accounting were so utterly ineffective as to make it impossible to say what the losses actually were. That man is a man who is called upon to report on the affairs of great corporations. Thousands of shareholders rely upon his statements. Those who are administrating estates relay on his statements. His statements are accepted as the basis of extremely important transactions in connection with the securities of those corporations. Is it to be, then, that his statements would be accepted with such finality in regard to methods of accounting in the ordinary case and be completely disregarded in a report of this kind, made to the government which appointed him and which stated that he was the best man in Canada for the job? I hope not.
I hope that, even with the willingness there has been to permit some doubt to creep in about the complete accuracy of his statements, at least there will be no attempt to create any impression that his statements in regard to methods of accounting and matters of that kind are challengeable at this time.
We have only seen through one window; and we were only allowed to look into one room. The room was so hopelessly untidy that we should know that the rest of the house must be just as untidy. Our job is to make sure there is a cleaning up of that house. Our job is to make sure that something will be done so that we can see in the other windows. If we cannot have more housecleaning by trained housecleaners then at least let us make sure some system is adopted which will assure housecleaning in the most important section of the whole operation; and the most important section of that operation is the operation of the air services.
We are not just dealing with air services because they are air services. We are not

just dealing with the suggestion that there should be an associate minister of defence for air because that challenges the imagination. We are dealing with it because it has been agreed on both sides of this house that Canada's primary contribution to the defence of our land, and to the common defence of freedom, is in the building up of our air forces. That is also before us in the extent to which allocation of funds is being directed to that department.
In the estimates tabled this week we find that for the year ending March 31, 1954, $332 million is to be spent for the navy, $533 million for the army, and $936 million for air defences. The latter figure is more than half of the total amount to be spent for all our defences. I would point out that this, of course, does not include the supplementary estimates which will add substantially to the figures.
The figures before us show that air defence calls for 52 [DOT] 5 per cent of our total expenditure for defence. The figure for army is 29-1 per cent, and for the navy it is 18 -4 per cent.
Therefore, air defences are of primary importance both from the point of view of their recognized importance as part of our combined defence activities and also from the point of view of the amount of money to be spent on them. That is the reason why we strongly urge the government to consider, even at this stage, its declared decision not to appoint a minister with definite authority to deal with air defence but rather simply to appoint a minister with general and undefined authority under the Minister of National Defence.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if there is one thing that we should bear in mind at the time we deal with this subject on this occasion it is that we are not just dealing with an ordinary legislative measure. We are dealing with the defence of our country. We are dealing with the enlistment, training, equipment, supply and direction of those young men and women in uniform who take the highest responsibility for the defence of Canada. Anything that has come to our attention which should be dealt with in regard to this subject should be dealt with on this occasion. We should not disregard these important matters when we are asked to amend the National Defence Act.
Instead of anything positive now before us we simply have a repetition of statements such as have been made on earlier occasions. As we deal with this subject at this time we must remember that instead of some positive declaration that radical changes are
National Defence Act
going to take place we simply have the assurance that we are going to continue the same methods we have used in the past. I cannot help but recall statements made in the House of Commons of Great Britain on May 25, 1938. They show how similar these problems are from time to time. They show how necessary it is for the mere civilian, elected as a member of parliament in this house, to deal with the problems of national defence and not leave them to the officers in charge, no matter how competent they may be. I would recall these statements by the present Prime Minister in Britain in the debate on the possibility of strengthening Britain's air defences at that time. He said then that in the House of Commons over there they had been reassured time and time again that everything was being done that should be done for the defence of Britain in the face of the German threat. He said that any suggestion of this kind is met with this sort of reply, and I quote:
That is being considered. We have given our attention to this. We are fully alive to that. The other matter is engaging our interested attention. We are exploring that.
I simply read those words to remind the members of this house that if there is one subject which, over and over again, has called for the attention of civilians in parliament it is the reorganization of the Department of National Defence and the abandonment of the old methods which have been carried over from the war before, whatever that war might be.
Every hon. member in this house will recall the statement that war is too serious a business to be left to staff officers. Now, that statement is not a reflection on staff officers. It is simply a statement of something that everyone knows who has had any dealing with this subject. The most efficient officers in war naturally regard the methods under which they were able to work satisfactorily as very useful and desirable methods. Naturally, those officers are inclined to perpetuate those methods and carry forward the same system. The more efficient they have been, the more certain they are that these methods are quite satisfactory.
There is not one occasion when reform in the system of administering our Department of National Defence, either in this country or in Great Britain, has come from staff officers. On every occasion it has come from consideration of the problem by parliament, with the advice of those who examined the matter from an objective and independent point of view. We even had the

National Defence Act
situation after the Napoleonic wars when Wellington himself was prime minister of Great Britain, yet he was not able to bring about those reforms which would give Britain an efficient army. Years later, when the Crimean war came, Britain still did not have an efficient army. It was not as a result of the recommendations of any staff officers following that war that reforms were brought about. In fact, they were not brought about, and many of the unsatisfactory conditions continued until a royal commission was appointed to inquire into the whole administration of the Ministry of Defence in Great Britain.
The Prime Minister, the members of the government, and most members in this house will recall the famous Esher commission which was the basis of a reorganization of the British army, and became the basis of our own reorganization of our defence forces in this country. The same thing happened after the great war. The reorganization which was obviously necessary was not brought about as a result of recommendations from members of the general staff. It was civilian organizations which pressed for reforms and were able to bring them into force. The reason for this has nothing to do with any intractability of mind on the part of the professional soldier. The professional soldier is answerable to the government. The professional soldier must take his direction from the government; he must carry out policies established by the government. It is not for him to tell the government what it will do; it is for the government to say what the staff officers will do and what the armed forces under those staff officers will do. That has been the policy of the supervision of our defence forces ever since we have had defence forces. The time has now come, therefore, when we should be considering this problem as civilian members of this parliament, and in the light of information which has come to us.
If there is one thing to which we should not agree, it is allowing habits of the past to stand in the way of reorganization which will be sound and effective in the light of the experience we have had in this house. In addition to the evidence of the breakdown in administration of the department, we also have before us the statement of the Auditor General that in spite of recommendations that something be done there are still eight different methods of accounting in that department. Those are the kind of things that should be tackled at this time. They are the kind of things we should be assured will be dealt with by any steps we now take. Instead of indicating to us how
[Mr: Drew.]
these problems are going to be solved, how this great expenditure of money is going to be managed in a way that will assure a higher measure of efficiency, we are asked to support a measure that simply says we will have another minister who will have the same duties as the minister already appointed.
