subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
What the government is asking us to do is to pass a bill which permits the appointment of an associate minister and then say, in effect, to the members of parliament: You trust us to use our judgment as to how this can best be done. I submit that this government should be prepared to accept the fact that the evidence before us demonstrates that it has not justified that responsibility. What is before us demonstrates the need for a measure containing the power not only to appoint a minister but to define in the most exact terms what his responsibility will be. We suggest that the responsibility should be defined, in any event, whether it is to be an associate minister of national defence for air or simply to provide the authority to appoint an associate minister.
There is, moreover, the fact that the Prime Minister has emphasized to us that it is not desirable that undefined powers should be granted. I do not profess to quote his exact words, but I am sure that this was the effect of what he said. I would hope that there would be as few occasions as possible when the executive would dispense with the authority of parliament in any matter of major importance. There are some of us who do regard the definition of the authority of this new minister as a matter of importance. That being so, I urge the Prime Minister to follow the very line that he has put before us, and to agree that it is not wise to dispense with the authority of parliament in a matter of such importance. We say there should be another minister. We say also that there should be another minister with definite powers. We say there should be an associate minister of defence for air. If the government is not prepared to go that far, the minister they appoint should have clear and definite responsibilities. Parliament has a responsibility for what is done on this occasion. I hope every member of parliament will keep in mind the facts that have been placed before us, the facts that are contained in the Currie report, and the facts that are contained in the report of the Auditor General, and the knowledge that we have

obtained from the minister himself that the present system is such that he did not even see any of the large number of reports that came forward recommending a better system of accounting in the particular part of the army that was under consideration at that time.
It is difficult to follow the Prime Minister's argument that it would create a lack of co-ordination if there were appointed an associate minister of defence for air when he told us that no problem arose in that connection previously. I would certainly be among the first to argue that we should not follow any other legislative body in the course they adopt simply because of the size or the importance of that body. Nevertheless I think we may well bear in mind the fact that the head of the government of the United States today is not only a man of demonstrated administrative ability but is one of the outstanding soldiers of our generation.
In his speech to congress just over two hours ago that man emphasized the importance of the allocation of responsibilities to associate officials for air, navy and other defence activities. This man who not only led the combined forces of the western world in Europe in the days of victory but also did so much to co-ordinate the defence forces of western Europe within the past few years believes it is wise to place the administration of air defence under an official who will be fully responsible for that matter to the minister of national defence. I submit that in this case it constitutes a strong argument.
However, we do not need to go to Washington for an argument. I think most of us will agree that Winston Churchill has demonstrated a fairly satisfactory knowledge of the administration of defence forces. He did so during the war. I should think that experience is useful today. He believes it is wise to have a separate minister responsible for air defence; and that man, with experience which contributed so greatly to the freedom that we possess today, has continued the administration of air defence under a separate minister of defence for air. Whether under our own system as in the United Kingdom or under the different system of the United States, at least it can be said that the two major powers in the western community of nations have decided that it is most efficient to have a minister of defence for air.
With this evidence before us; with the evidence of the need for a clear definition of responsibility; and with the clear evidence of the need to relieve the present minister of a substantial measure of responsibility if the
National Defence Act
confusion in and ineffectiveness of that department are to be overcome, I submit that we should be dealing with an act which will appoint not only a minister but one with defined authority.
On second reading I do not believe it would be necessary for us to attempt to define that authority; it will be possible for us to do so when this measure goes into committee. However, on second reading it is possible to ask for a reconsideration of this measure and, in the light of what has been said, in the light of the statements of the Prime Minister himself, who has told us that no difficulty arose, even under the pressure of war, in defining the limits of responsibility of associate ministers and separate ministers appointed in this way, to ask the government to reconsider and bring before us a bill that will provide for the appointment of a minister of defence for air with clearly defined authority approved by this parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes):
That the said bill be not now read the second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introducing of legislation to amend the National Defence Act which will provide for one or more associate ministers with duties defined by statute.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two or three things on which I think both the government and the members of the opposition are agreed. I would say that the first is that there is need for a reorganization of the Department of National Defence. It is quite evident that the government agree in view of the fact that they bring in this amendment. They agree that there has been lack of proper supervision- not altogether because of the Minister of National Defence but because of the multiple duties which have been placed on him during the last few years-and that some assistance is necessary.
In the second place, there is need for more detailed examination by the civil authorities of the expenditures which take place in the Department of National Defence. That fact is perfectly evident from the Currie report and from letters which almost every member of parliament gets from day to day with regard to the detailed operations of the Department of National Defence. The point on which we seem to disagree is how this assistance shall be given to the department and how we can get a more efficient administration of the department to supervise these tremendous expenditures which the Department of National Defence is making today.

National Defence Act
I think that the Prime Minister probably gave the best arguments that could be given to the house for a minister or an associate minister with defined responsibilities. He stated that during the war we had two associate ministers of national defence and that they found no difficulty in administering their departments through a minister in that department. The reason they found so few difficulties was simply that they had clearly-defined responsibilities. The minister for air had the responsibility for air, the minister for the navy had responsibility for the navy, and so on. They had clearly defined responsibilities and they were therefore able to carry on in an efficient and effective way.
In any large business today, those in authority must have clearly-defined responsibility if the business is to be a success. How we can expect to operate the Department of National Defence-which is the largest spending department of the government-with an associate minister without any clearly-defined responsibilities is beyond my comprehension. It does not make common business sense.
In any large business where you are spending hundreds of millions of dollars someone must be responsible for that spending. Here we have an associate minister being appointed without any defined responsibility. To me that does not make sense, and I do not think it will make sense to many people across the country.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that if he appointed an associate minister for air, this inevitably would mean that we would have to appoint an associate deputy minister for air. Well, why not?
Just what will be the position of the deputy minister of national defence when he has two bosses. He has a difficult enough time now with one boss. He has not been able to report to that boss all the things that are happening in the department. I do not see how it will help to appoint another associate minister to whom the deputy would have to report, unless he is given some assistance as well. The deputy minister of national defence has terrific responsibilities, almost equalling those of the minister. By appointing an associate minister, and failing to appoint a deputy under him, I just cannot see how it will solve the difficulty with which we are faced.
I agree that any minister of the crown should have clearly defined responsibilities. I know of no occasion in the Canadian parliament when we have appointed ministers and have not clearly defined their responsibilities. When during the war we appointed associate ministers of national defence they were made responsible for particular departments. The

minister for air was responsible for air; the minister for the navy was responsible for the navy, and the then minister of national defence was responsible for the army. Naturally the senior associate minister became responsible for the whole department, in the absence of the minister when he had to go abroad or to be absent from parliament on other business.
That seems a natural division. It is a workable division of responsibility. But if we have an associate minister with no defined responsibility, and no deputy minister under him, it seems to me we are just going to add to the confusion we already have in the Department of National Defence, as evidenced by the Currie report and the report of the Auditor General.
Surely the government is anxious to see that that situation is cleared up. I think the most effective way of doing it would be to appoint an associate minister for air, with defined responsibility, and a deputy minister under him who could carry out the supervision of the tremendous air expenditures we are making today. Not only are we making these expenditures on behalf of the Canadian people, but we are bringing to Canada young airmen from other NATO countries, training them here, and supplying them with some of the equipment they will have to use when they go back to their own countries, and operate in connection with the common defence problem with which the world is faced today. Surely that problem is important enough that we in Canada should have an associate minister for air, with defined responsibility, and a deputy minister under him who could carry out his orders, and thus have the proper supervision we should have in the department.
I am not going to labour the matter; but I do think if the government were wise, if it were anxious to have the best possible administration, this can be done only when we have an associate minister with clearly defined responsibilities. No business organization in Canada could operate successfully under two bosses, one of whom had no clearly defined responsibilities.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word about this bill. I listened to what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had to say this afternoon, and it seemed to me he found it pretty difficult to justify the proposal he put forward. I wondered at the time if the provisions in the bill were what had been recommended to him by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). That may account for the difficulty he had in justifying

his position. It seemed to me at one stage particularly that the Prime Minister was arguing against himself.
If we pass this bill and proceed to appoint an associate minister of national defence, with no definite powers and responsibilities, then in case something arises again as has already arisen in the army works services, we would never be able to pin anyone down. We would have put these ministers in a position where they could blame each other. And if that occurs, then what chance have we to pin them down and place responsibility where it should be placed?
If we proceeded to do what has already been suggested, that is appoint an associate minister for air and define his powers carefully in the legislation, then we would have something specific and could hold someone responsible if things went wrong.
I have not been able to understand the amendment very well. The one that was handed to me makes reference to estimates for the year ending March 31, 1954, and then it proceeds to outline what the army, navy and air force is supposed to get by way of appropriations. I take it for granted this is not what was supposed to be amended. Under the circumstances I have to rely upon my memory. But I think it is reasonable to suggest that the government should withdraw the bill as it is now, and bring back a bill which would provide for the appointment of an associate minister for air. That is what we favour.
Speaking when the resolution was before the house, our spokesman suggested that we should accept the proposal of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) that there be such a minister with defined powers. I join the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in making that suggestion today.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this measure was being discussed in the resolution stage I think there was general agreement on all sides of the house that the time had arrived, if indeed it was not actually overdue, when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) should be given some additional help in the execution of his many and great responsibilities.
I am not going to enter into a discussion as to whether this procedure, as indicated in the bill, is actually necessary or not. It was stated clearly earlier this afternoon that a state of urgency does actually exist. However, in seconding the amendment offered by the leader of this party I do wish to review the request I made during the debate at the resolution stage that there should be a clearer definition of the duties of the associate minister.
National Defence Act
Speaking at the resolution stage the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) indicated that the associate minister would be responsible for the administrative details relative to the three services. He gave, as he did this afternoon, some details as to what those administrative duties would be. They would be rather vague responsibilities connected with the general administration of the three services.
I suggest that the duties of the associate minister as we have them at present will be those of a super-parliamentary assistant. He has already been occupying the position of a parliamentary assistant, and to a certain extent will be carrying out those general administrative supervisions. That is not really what is required. Even though you give a man a different title you cannot expect him to give greater assistance than he has been able to give in the past unless you him some additional and clearly defined responsibility.
As an alternative to the vague duties that he is to perform in regard to the administration of the three services, I suggested during the resolution stage that there should be appointed an associate minister for air. I do not mind whether you refer to him as the minister for air or the associate minister for air, because there is no appreciable difference to my way of thinking. The associate minister for air or the minister for air must be associated with the Minister of National Defence, whose responsibility quite obviously would be to co-ordinate the activities of the minister or associate minister for air.
When speaking on January 22 the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) offered as a reason why it might be difficult for a separate minister for air or an associate minister for air to carry out his duties apart from those of the Minister of National Defence that it was necessary for arrangements to be made for the establishment of airfields and barracks in France for the R.C.A.F., and that the arrangements so made would have a bearing on the discussions going on in Germany and Belgium in connection with our army units now stationed in those countries. He then went on to say that those arrangements would have to be negotiated by one minister.
Of course they would have to be negotiated by one minister. The Prime Minister also pointed out on January 22 that the Minister of National Defence would have to attend to matters having to do with defence relationships with the United Nations and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The Minister of National Defence would be performing the very same duties he has had

National Defence Act
to perform heretofore, but he would have more time to devote to those international defence relationships, be they with the United Kingdom or with NATO. He would coordinate the activities of the three defence services. He would have to co-ordinate the negotiations for these airfields and barracks, be they required for the army or the navy.
I cannot see any difficulty about that. That is what he is going to do in any case. After all, these matters have been discussed at length at the various conferences which the Minister of National Defence has been attending recently and they are all summed up in a rather difficult word, "infrastructure". It is the infrastructure of NATO in Europe which takes care of these housekeeping details for the troops of the various nations, including Canada, which are at present serving in Europe for the defence of western ideals. Therefore I see nothing out of the way as far as that suggestion is concerned.
The Minister of National Defence would co-ordinate the activities of the minister or associate minister for air. Since we made those recommendations on January 22 I think the attention of this nation has been directed toward the importance of the air services in a most pronounced way. The services of the chief of the air staff, Air Marshal W.
A.	Curtis, terminated at the end of last week. In an impressive ceremony in his farewell to the force which he had done so much to build up he called attention to the pre-eminent position of the R.C.A.F. in the general defence structure of this nation. He went so far as to say that the Canadian people and even parliament did not realize the revolution which had been taking place in this country's military structure.
I wonder whether the government has realized the tremendous changes which have been taking place over the past few years in so far as the relationship of the air services to the other forces of this country are concerned. I cannot help recalling that in 1949 I made the statement in this house that for every dollar spent on the army three dollars should be spent on the air force. I was told that I had gone too far, that the suggestion I had made was quite impracticable.
I based my recommendation at that time on the fact that in 1947-48 the amount spent on the air force was $55 million out of a total defence expenditure of $195 million, and that in 1948-49, $90 million was being allocated to the air force out of a total of $268 million. I appealed to the minister to face with immediate determination the problem which was before him and if necessary to act ruthlessly in the reorganization of the forces, only to be met, as I have
[Mr. Pearkes.l
said already, with the statement that my suggestion was impracticable. I was told that if my suggestion were brought into effect a sum of $600 million would have to be allocated for the air force alone.
Today we have gone far beyond that amount. Today the sum of approximately $1 billion is being allocated to the air force. If the amount I suggested, $600 million, had been allocated at that time it would have meant, according to the minister, an expenditure of $3 on the air force for every $1 spent on the army. Well, we have exceeded that. I wonder whether we have really realized the extent of the evolution that has been taking place. The retiring air marshal uses these words, as found in a report of his speech in the Montreal Gazette:
The. fact we have sent large expeditionary forces overseas in two wars to fight on the ground has left its mark on Canadian thinking. It has tended to obscure the fact that both our human and industrial resources, or small but skilled population and our complex industry, fit us for concentration on air power. It has also obscured the fact that we are already tending in that direction to a marked degree. Other countries have the manpower for massed ground warfare. We haven't. But we do have the technical skills, the high level of education and the industrial establishment to support a relatively large air force because its manpower demands are much less and are of the type we can meet admirably.
He went on to say:
This by no means indicates a lessening of our contribution to joint defence.
Then he gives as an example the fact that in the near future we will have some 7,000 airmen in Europe and that that will be approximately the same number as there are in the army units in Europe. Then he made this very pertinent statement:
The airmen will have at their command roughly ten times the striking power of the soldiers.
I think that is an indication of the important role which the Royal Canadian Air Force is now playing not only in the defence of Canada but in the carrying out of the obligations that Canada has assumed in other parts of the world. If more than half of this year's total defence estimates are to be spent on air services, surely it indicates that the spending of that large amount of money on that most important service requires a minister who can concentrate upon the development and construction of the new types of aircraft which the retiring air marshal indicated have already been started in this country, even though they have not yet got beyond the planning stage.
As he pointed out, we must have a new type of fighter ready and available by 1960 at which time he indicated that the CF-100, which is not yet fully in service, would be

obsolete. Therefore I feel that with all these important developments that are taking place in this field we must be quite certain that we are developing our air services and air equipment along the right lines. There is the vast field of guided missiles, be they ground to air or air to air, which must be explored and developed.
I believe the air services constitute a tremendous field which will require the full attention of a cabinet minister who will devote practically all his time to looking after the interests of that service. I do not care whether that minister is called a minister or an associate minister. That is immaterial; but let us avoid this duplication, the continuance of this confusion that has existed in the past few years and which will continue if we merely appoint an associate minister who will carry on general duties of administration in such an ill-defined manner as has been described today.
It has been suggested that a minister is required to recommend the allocation of funds and of manpower among the three services, and that if there were three separate ministers there would be competition between them for whatever funds were available. We have seen that competition in past years. Certainly we saw it in pre-war days when there were three chiefs of staff, each of them competing for such funds as were available. But I am not suggesting that. No suggestion has ever been made that there should be three separate ministers all of equal rank. We have emphasized the importance-and I repeat it- of there being a co-ordinating authority, a minister who is responsible for co-ordinating the activities of the three services, for coordinating the purchases of airfields in Europe or the allocation of funds among the various services in Canada. That would be a general supervisory minister, who would be responsible for the supervision of the services.
I believe that situation exists in the United Kingdom at the present time. It certainly has in the past. There is a minister of defence, but under that minister there can be other ministers definitely responsible for certain particular duties in connection with the services. I am suggesting that there should be someone with definite responsibility for developing our air services which today are pre-eminent and are taking up more than 50 per cent of the funds allocated for defence. It is not fair to suggest that senior staff officers of the various services would be able to make their representations in such a way that they could be properly weighed by the government.
It has already been pointed out that the senior staff officers of the various services
National Defence Act
are the servants of the government. They must carry out the policy of the government. In the past, as I said earlier, there has been competition between the three services. Today I think there are three chiefs of staff and I presume there is a certain amount of competition between them; but a chairman of the chiefs of staff committee has been appointed and I presume that it is partly his duty to co-ordinate requests which are made by the different chiefs of staff.
So in seconding this motion I do stress the desirability of giving and placing on the statute books clearly defined instructions to this associate minister of national defence whom we all agree is necessary in order to assist the present minister in the fulfilment of his duties.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few observations I would like to make with regard to the subject which is now before the house for discussion. Over the last few years defence spending has increased to such an extent that the Department of National Defence is spending nearly half of the national budget. There is increasing evidence to indicate that concurrently with this great increase in spending and great increase in responsibility the ministry of defence is becoming so large and unwieldy as to be unmanageable.
I think the problem is generally recognized, and it is also recognized that the responsibilities are too great to rest on the shoulders of only one minister. I think it is obviously unreasonable to have one minister in the government spending almost as much as all other ministers put together. Therefore it seems obvious that something in the way of appointing another minister to share this great load of responsibility is a necessary step, and one that we have to face.
Before plunging off in any particular direction on the problem and how it should be solved or met, it might be well to look briefly at what has been done in other countries; because they too have met these very problems. We find in the United Kingdom that for many years they have had three ministers responsible for the three services. This is also the case in the commonwealth of Australia. There at the present time there is a defence minister responsible for the co-ordination of defence generally, and they also have a minister for the army and another minister responsible for the air force and the navy.
In the United Kingdom, as I have already said, there are three ministers who are responsible for the services. There it has been recognized that by dividing responsibility between various ministers you may lose a

National Defence Act
certain amount of co-ordination. That is a problem that must be faced, and I think we all recognize that problem. In the United Kingdom an attempt has been made to solve it by appointing a minister of defence who is responsible for the co-ordination of defence generally. This procedure takes from the Prime Minister in a general way the load of responsibility for defence.
I would like to quote briefly from a white paper published by the United Kingdom government in 1946 with regard to the central organization for defence on the occasion when it was considered necessary to appoint a defence minister. It says:
Outline of new organization proposed
After reviewing the development of our defence organization over the last forty years and its practical performance under the test of two major wars, His Majesty's government are satisfied that there are no grounds for any drastic recasting of the main structure of the organization as it exists today. Some changes are, however, required in order to consolidate the advances which have been made in recent years under the compulsion of war or of the threat of war. Above all, experience during these years has shown the need of a minister who has both the time and the authority to formulate and apply a unified defence policy for the three services; and it is proposed that this need should be met by the creation of a minister of defence.
That is the position in the United Kingdom. They have a minister of defence responsible for defence and for the co-ordination of the various defence departments; but in addition they have ministers directly responsible to parliament who have clearly defined fields of responsibility, and their fields of responsibility coincide with the various services in the United Kingdom. The paper goes on to say:
The service ministers will continue to be responsible to parliament for the administration of their services in accordance with the general policy approved by the cabinet and within the resources allotted to them.
That is what I would consider a reasonable solution to the problem and it would seem to me that here in Canada we should go very carefully before we start branching off on some new and unproven idea. I think we should try to retain the principle where each minister has clearly defined responsibilities. In Australia, as I have said, that is accomplished by having a defence minister and separate ministers, one responsible for the army, and one for the air force and navy. Of course, it does not necessarily follow that we should completely follow either one of those systems, but I think we can learn a good deal from them.
If we look at the expenditures of the Department of National Defence we find that more than one-fifth of our total budget is
[Mr. MacLean (Queens) .1
now spent by the air force, and almost one-half of our budget is spent by the Department of National Defence. It would seem, on that basis, to be reasonable to have a minister responsible for the co-ordination of defence generally and also responsible for the army and navy, with another minister responsible for the air force who might be called the associate minister of defence for air, or something of that sort.
The Prime Minister in his remarks pointed out that if such a system were introduced you would have the problem of requiring to create some new positions such as another deputy minister. He pointed out that this would necessitate further expenditures, and that economy is a very important thing. I agree with the Prime Minister and I think his sentiments along that line are most commendable, but I think that at the same time we might easily fall into the danger of being penny wise and pound foolish. After all, why should one deputy minister be considered capable of supervising and carefully vetting expenditures representing half our national budget when it takes perhaps twenty other deputy ministers to look after the remainder.
I think this is a case where perhaps money could be saved by the appointment of another deputy minister. In any case I think it should be very important to have a clear line drawn between the responsibilities of the minister of defence and those of the associate minister of defence or whatever you may wish to call him. The important thing is that each one should have a watertight compartment of responsibility so far as parliament is concerned.
Although I do not think it is vitally important that the responsibility should be divided in precisely that way, I think there is a good argument for it. In addition to our air force spending about one-fifth of our national budget, the Department of National Defence, if its existence is justified at all, exists to deal with any war or threat of war which may come our way in the future. If there is a real threat of war or if there is another war, the defence of this country will be, for the most part, air defence. Any other activities in which we might engage with our armed forces will be more or less military mutual aid. So far as the defence of this continent is concerned it will be primarily a case of air defence. So far as the actual defence of Canada is concerned, that responsibility will rest to a great degree upon the air force. I believe that is another reason why the appointment of an associate minister

responsible for the air defence of our country, as well as other activities of the Department of National Defence, is reasonable.
I believe that at this time the government proposes we should create the position of associate minister of defence without defining precisely what his responsibilities are going to be. In other words, we are going to have one Department of National Defence and two ministers. We will have one body with two heads. Before we create a monstrosity of that sort we should give the matter careful consideration. After all, you are going to have one servant and two masters, a department of defence and two ministers. I believe it is generally recognized that it is impossible to serve two masters. You are going to create a sort of two-headed hydra. I think we should be very careful before we put such a monster on the payroll.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
It seems to be the general opinion that the proposal before the house this afternoon is long overdue. All hon. members who have taken part in the debate thus far agree with the general principle that some further administrative assistance is necessary in the Department of National Defence.
There is no need for me to labour what has already been said during the discussion this afternoon, and the other discussions that have taken place here in recent weeks. In rising to take part in this debate I should like to emphasize a point that has been raised by the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), to the effect that the solution of the difficulty is not in establishing a vague assistanceship but rather that the duties of the assistant minister be clearly defined under the heading of associate minister for air.
We realize that the responsibility of the Department of National Defence has been accentuated by the Korean crisis, and the position is extremely difficult mainly because we are in a twilight war period which makes it hard indeed to stir up the response of the public to the demands and responsibilities that are created by such a situation. We acknowledge and recognize that the problem of administering matters pertaining to the army and the navy are extremely difficult. However, I feel it is obvious that Canada has a peculiar natural situation so far as air force matters are concerned, and that the present situation confronting the western powers necessitates that Canada carry forward with the greatest possible speed and efficiency the program of air defence upon which she has embarked. During world war II it became firmly established in the minds
National Defence Act
of military authorities that air power was absolutely indispensable to the successful conclusion of any military campaign. In fact some authorities, I recall, went out on the limb a considerable distance by recommending that the only way to achieve victory in modern warfare was through air power. We had such presentations appearing under such titles as "Victory through air power". Whether or not that be true, I am not going to discuss this afternoon.
We do know that, because of the geographic position in which Canada finds herself, because of the nature of the country, it is essential that she make a major effort toward solving the very difficult problems confronting her at the present time in regard to the build-up of air power. It has been pointed out that today almost $1 billion is being expended in air force expansion, and that represents almost one-half our total expenditure for defence. In that factor alone we have emphasized the necessity for giving special attention to the appointment of some individual who would be particularly responsible for the administration of the expenditure of this huge sum of money.
In addition to the peculiar situation of Canada, as is recognized in the amount of money that is being granted for air force matters, we have the record that was established by the R.C.A.F. during world war II. This record speaks for itself, but I believe that the success that was achieved by our air force was second to none, commencing almost from scratch in 1939. That achievement was largely due to the fact that there was one minister who had the burden of carrying through the very extensive and difficult program of expansion.
There is another matter related to the problem of air defence. Actually I suppose it comes under the heading of defence production. In connection with the tremendous build-up that is facing our Canadian air force, there has been some discussion in the house concerning the lack of success in the industrial part of the program. For example, there have been discussions concerning the progress made in the production of Canada's CF-100, the much heralded all-weather fighter which is now, according to reports, in the production stage. I feel that some of the discussion has arisen from lack of information, or it might be from undue optimism expressed in the reports we have had in the chamber. Some of this discussion has been unfortunate, because if we had actually realized the problems connected with the development of an original aircraft type from the drawing board stage to actual production, some of the criticism would not

National Defence Act have been brought forward in the house. The same thing applies, of course, to the Orenda engine.
I was thumbing through the pages of the magazine Aircraft for March, 1952, and the writer makes much the same point as I have just made. In reference to the CF-100 he says that admittedly the production of the CF-100 is behind schedule at A. V. Roe (Canada) Limited . . . there is much to indicate that in the eagerness to promise that the R.C.A.F. would build up strength in a remarkably short time, the government was prone to an overly-optimistic view of how soon the CF-100 could be made available.
Optimistic prognostications of that kind have led to unnecessary criticism. With a responsible minister in charge of air force matters-and the need is becoming increasingly obvious-who was able to find the time to keep closely in touch with the production aspects of the building up of our air force, statements of that kind could be avoided; because overly-optimistic statements tend to arise from a lack of detailed information on the inevitable problems that must be faced when we are in the process of establishing our own aircraft industry. As another example-and others could be mentioned

we have the experience with the jet liner on which some $6 million was expended in the production of an original prototype of Canadian manufacture. Then suddenly the project was dropped in the interests of more pressing demands for aircraft of military type. If there had been proper co-ordination and planning, and if there had been one minister responsible for the handling of the complex matters pertaining to the air force, no doubt this expenditure could have been avoided.
It is most interesting to note that recently Canada has placed an order for two of the British Comets as soon as they become available. Whether this action is the result of careful forethought as to what use these Comet air liners might be put to in the air force, or whether again it is a case of jumping oft into the dark and hoping they might be useful, still remains to be seen. We have not heard any discussion on that point.
So far as the air force is concerned, the crux of the matter is that we are in what you might call almost a revolutionary period in air power development. During world war II Canada established an enviable record. As I have indicated, she developed a tremendously effective and powerful air force in a relatively short space of time. But looking back now on the experience of world war II and the types of aircraft then used, we find that even the best types have today become completely obsolescent. We find ourselves in a major period of change, a transitional
[Mr. Dinsdale.l

period, that is demanding not only the development of new aircraft types but also new techniques in the handling of the new aircraft, and an entirely new approach to the problem of air offensive and air defence.
With the tremendous multiple tasks involved in proceeding successfully without a repetition of some of the costly errors into which we have fallen, it seems to me it is essential that as we move to tighten up defence department administration we should give special attention to the air force department by the appointment of an associate minister who will have complete responsibility for the successful carrying out of the transitional period developments.
I could have mentioned another example of misunderstanding caused by lack of information. For a long time in this house we were pursuing the question of the use of -5 calibre armament that was almost obsolescent in world war II. Of course the difficulty there was that it was merely stopgap armament, and that we were moving forward into guided missiles and other armament developments which are still on the highly secret list. This being so I repeat that there is an urgent necessity that some specialized attention be given to air force matters if we, as a Canadian air force, are going to maintain the record that we established in world war II and if we are going to play the role that is demanded of this country as we participate in NATO defence and in the defence of western Christian civilization generally.
There is one more point I should like to raise while I have the opportunity to do so. In addition to the need to have highly competent guidance in this transitional period, I think there are many indications that point to the necessity for a more judicious and economical use of manpower. As we have been endeavouring to build up the air force potential again-I think we had declined in total numerical strength to something like
14,000	in 1947, and since that time we have come back to almost 50,000-the emphasis in recruiting has been to establish a core of qualified personnel to carry on the necessary training operations. As I have endeavoured to get information on this matter of recruiting, it has seemed to me that it has been a difficult and painful process to get candidates of the right kind to link up with our air force. We have resorted to the use of "retreads" as they are popularly known, or men with world war II experience retrained and brought back into the service in order to meet the immediate demands of the extended activity. Not only in the active force but in connection with the reserves we find a good deal of uncertainty in this regard. It seems no one has

sat down and considered how reserve skills and experience could be used most expeditiously and efficiently.
I happen to be associated with an air force association. This is a voluntary group of air force veterans banded together to assist the air force in every way possible in maintaining its high standards and also in meeting the challenge of the present emergency period. The association to which I belong in the city of Brandon happens to be recognized as the banner association because of the excellent work it has done in the last year. However, constantly we feel frustrated because we have a feeling that we are not tying directly into the demands of the present emergency situation. The numerical strength of the wing is high, but there is no concrete program, other than that of assisting in recruiting. They had thought they might assist as an air observation corps, but there is going to be no need for that particular activity in our area.
Along with a failure to make expeditious and efficient use of reserve skills and experience, we find that some of our air force associations are not up to date in meeting the demands of air force expansion. It seems to me that with a minister responsible for air, more detailed attention could be given to the peculiar problems of recruiting in this country. Where we have a voluntary system, specialized attention must be given to putting the idea across to potential candidates so they will know that the air force requires their services. Instead of inducing volunteers to enter our services by promising them personal security with pensions and the like, we should put it across to them as a direct challenge to assist in the preservation of our way of life.
Actually if the emergency situation is as severe as we think it is, and if the comments we hear respecting the discussions that took place at NATO in the early part of January are true-and it will be recalled that our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) took part in those discussions-then we are facing a real emergency that demands the promptest attention we can possibly give to the problem of establishing our own air force. For example, I believe it was the Ottawa Journal of Monday, January 26, which stated that a responsible officer of high rank in the United States army said that a surprise allout Russian air attack would knock out western Europe's first line of air defence in one swoop.
If that is so, rather than thinking in terms of a minimum of defence we should be thinking in terms of a maximum. This is particularly true in Canada, which is in the direct
National Defence Act
line of attack between the potential enemy and the target to the south of us that would have highest priority. This means that almost all of us are in the front line and that in every way possible, by means of information to the press and so on, we should try to impress upon those who are in the reserves and who have had experience in the air force that they are needed to assist in establishing what will become the front line of defence, our air power.
To sum up these remarks, I am glad to see that steps are going to be taken to solve a problem that has become increasingly difficult. In fact, ever since I came to the House of Commons the Department of National Defence has been under attack and criticism for some cause or another. In most cases the criticism has arisen from a genuine feeling that all was not for the best in this particular department. I do not think, however, that the appointment of a glorified parliamentary assistant, as the present proposal seems to suggest, is a solution. I feel there is a special need in Canada to give specific and particular attention to the problems faced by our air force as we move through this difficult transition period.
As for the argument that unification is the prime essential in matters of defence, I cannot agree because in my view this is a day of specialization, diversification and division of labour. In almost every industrial activity we find this diversification and specialization carried out to an extreme degree. Certainly if we can operate successfully with a division of labour to bring about greater efficiency in private business, we can operate just as successfully in government departments, and particularly in the field of national defence. We have the administrative skills; we have the business knowledge required to maintain the channels of communication that would be necessary if there were an appointment of a special minister for air.
As for the argument that additional expense would be involved, let me say that I think there is a very simple answer when one asks the rhetorical question: What could be more expensive than the present set-up in the Department of National Defence? This department has revealed a high degree of inefficiency mainly, I feel, because of the attempt of too few people to cover too much ground. Particularly is this true in the field of air power.
Then finally there is the appeal that the proposed scheme put forward by the government be given a fair trial. I do not think it merits consideration, because certainly during the last three years, through a process of

National Defence Act
trial and error, we have been attempting to meet the challenge facing us; and that process of trial and error has not worked out too satisfactorily. I would say that today is the time for action, particularly in matters pertaining to this very important part of our defence system, the Royal Canadian Air Force.

Mr. Speaker, I only wish to add a few words to the remarks made by those who have spoken before me during the debate on the bill now before the house providing for a most important amendment to the National Defence Act.
Not being a soldier, I must confess immediately my complete ignorance of the whole technical aspect of the various military divisions of national defence, such as the air force, the army and the navy. However, I fully support the remarks that have been made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) who asked for a clearer definition of the responsibilities, powers, duties, privileges and prerogatives of the associate minister of national defence, whose appointment is provided for in the bill now before the house.
Mr. Speaker, although fully realizing that the new associate minister will be indirectly responsible to the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), I am wondering if we must presume that the new associate minister will also be responsible to this house, that is to the hon. members who sit here as the representatives of the Canadian people; I am wondering also if the new associate minister of national defence would be just as responsible to -this house as the present Minister of National Defence-if not more so-because, after all, Mr. Speaker, in my estimation, one of the most important duties of any minister of the crown is to account for his actions to this house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF ASSOCIATE MINISTER OF NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
When the house took recess I had just made a brief reference to unification and co-ordination. This has particular

relevance to the bill under discussion because it is necessary to consider any further development in the organization of the national defence department and the appointment of an associate minister or other ministers against the background of what has been done. It is also necessary to have in mind the general desirability, I think admitted by all members, of securing the greatest possible unification and co-ordination of the activities of the three armed forces-the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian army and the Royal Canadian Air Force-as well as defence research.
In this connection I think hon. members opposite would agree that, all things being equal, it is a good thing to have the utmost possible unification and co-ordination, not for their own sake but because they produce better planning, better programs and greater economy. The hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White) speaking on March 14, 1950, as reported in Hansard at page 753 said:
I believe it is most important that Canada eliminate this duplication of services, and develop more efficiency, so far as it is possible, in our defence forces.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) said on May 16, 1950, as reported at page 2560 of Hansard:
It is to be hoped that unification will bring about a lessening of the amount of money which might be required for each of the services if they were to continue to operate separately.
The same hon. member on May 8, 1951, said at page 2809 of Hansard:
A co-ordinated or unified policy, though the various services may at times have to go through a slimming process, is far more likely to produce economical and effective results than is a system under which each of the services is working on its own.
With all those statements I emphatically agree, and I am sure the hon. members who made them would make them again.
In this connection what we tried to do was arrive at a basis of organization for the department under which plans and programs and the action necessary to carry them out would be taken by the department acting as a single department, having regard to the objects and necessities of the three services, but all within the lines of policy approved by the government. To a very considerable degree we have arrived at that objective. We have a unified system for preparing estimates, for establishing conditions of service, of standards of accommodation and the other items that enter into the production of estimates. I could also enumerate, if hon. members were interested and if time permitted, the ways in which unification has actually been carried out, duplication avoided, and coordination effected. However, most of those
National Defence Act
matters have already been put on Hansard and I will not delay the house with regard to them.
When the program of the Department of National Defence comes to be considered each year by the chiefs of staff committee there are present, in addition to the three chiefs of staff, the chairman of the defence research board, the deputy minister of national defence and, when required, representatives of the departments of external affairs, finance, and defence production. Questions are dealt with having regard to the agreed lines of government policy and within those lines it has usually proved possible, certainly in recent years, for the chiefs of staff and their committee, with representation such as I have described, to agree, and I say agree, on an allocation of the total amount to be provided for defence expenditure.
This is done by them and then the defence program as reflected in these estimates is considered in detail by a screening committee within the department where the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, the deputy minister, and representatives of the Department of Finance-treasury-go over the program in detail with each chief of staff in turn together with his officials responsible for making up the estimates. It is then referred to me and the whole program is put forward for approval by the cabinet defence committee and by the cabinet itself.
So I think you will find that to a very considerable extent we have effected that degree of unification and co-ordination which has been our objective, and which has been the objective of other countries. We have, under the system adopted since 1946, a single department, a single deputy minister, a single set of civil servants, a number of unified operations-all those relating to the civil service and a good many relating to the armed forces themselves. We have established identical conditions of service for all three services; for pay, allowances, pensions, food, clothing in so far as it is common to all services, transportation, leave arrangements, married quarters and the like. Also we have a single National Defence Act and a single disciplinary code. As I say, I think without fear of successful challenge, we have gone farther in the degree of unification, co-ordination and elimination of duplication than any country I know of.
All the time this has been going on we have been observing and studying what has gone on in other countries and, where it has

National Defence Act
been possible to learn from anything that has happened there, we have taken advantage of those developments.
It seems to me that on the principle of the Prime Minister's bill and the suggestions made by various opposition members, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has covered the question in general terms and I do not propose to go over that at all.
However, if the suggestion were adopted of having a separate minister or associate minister for air, then we would be limiting his activities because he would, under that proposal, act for air only. While I recognize the importance of the air branch, as other members do, I should point out that from the point of view of administration and the time occupied, the problems arising in connection with the air force are certainly no greater and probably less-though not in importance or amount of money spent-than the problems arising in connection with the army. You can appreciate this, because I think the air force has about one-fifth the number of units that the army has. It certainly has far less than one-fifth the number of weapons, and certainly less than one-fifth the number of contracts, due to different functions and operations.
If an order is placed for an aircraft like the CF-100 or the F-86E Sabre and its spare parts, then that order, subject to modification of course, is one operation which adds up to several hundred million dollars. It has to be watched carefully; but to add up to several hundred million dollars in terms of army equipment, construction and personnel requires a much greater number of administrative operations. If the proposed additional minister were to be limited to the air, then you would deprive the navy and army of his services unless the Minister of National Defence happened to be away. I believe that to return to the position where we have a Minister of National Defence and an associate minister earmarked for a special department would be a retrograde step. Indeed, the experience of other countries has shown that the best practice is to have either one minister or four.
If you had four ministers you would have, as in the United States, Britain or Australia, four departments. You not only would have a Department of National Defence but also one for the navy, one for the army and one for the air force. You would have to have all the things that go with a government department. There then would be the necessity of reconciling their programs, allocating funds, conditions of service and the like, all of which problems are avoided if you have a

single department. I suggest to hon. members that we have armed forces of the size, and a country of the size, which enables one department to handle the matter successfully. The proposal that we have an associate minister of national defence for air, I suggest, does not meet the needs as they exist today.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has put these things before you. I can assure you that I can say for the Solicitor General (Mr. Campney), or any other minister who might be appointed as associate, that there will not be duplication of effort nor confusion but there will be that kind of co-operation which is necessary to make for teamwork. I believe that the Prime Minister's proposal should be carried through.

I will be as brief as I can.
Having regard to what the minister said about the audit, I think I must ask the house to listen while I read the words in the Currie report, although they have been read before. I cannot make my argument unless I read what was said in this report with regard to the audit. At page 712 of Hansard for December 15, 1952, I find the following:

Having done that, he appears to think that his duty was done, and therefore he says there was no failure in that respect, notwithstanding these devastating words. Then I come to the recommendations in the Currie report. Some ten days ago or more the minister said in this house, I thought with some pride, that a lot of the recommendations of the Currie report had been put into effect. Well, Mr. Speaker, I find myself distressed by this because it seems to me that it indicates that in spite of everything the minister does not yet feel there is any real reason for correcting anything in the department. All I can say is if that is his real feeling, then it does not seem to me to make much difference whether we appoint one associate minister or a dozen associate ministers. It seems 68108-99

the minister like water over a duck's back, the situation disturbs me more than I can say.

Mr. Chairman, it would appear that there has been some misapprehension about the point to which I was directing my remarks. I propose to move an amendment, and my remarks are directed to the reason why an amendment should be made.
I am suggesting that the amendment that is to be proposed is one that is in keeping with the responsibilities of this house to the members of the armed forces. I would hope that in dealing with that there will be no recurrence of any suggestion that, when we make this proposal that there be a more efficient manner of administering the Department of National Defence, and that the government assume that measure of responsibility indicated by the facts placed before us, this is in any way a reflection on the members of the armed forces.
The members of the armed forces are those who deserve immediate action to improve the situation which now exists. That situation is one which calls for some change in the general procedure and improvement in the handling of national defence. These remarks are not directed to a minister now holding a portfolio. They are directed to the Prime Minister as head of the government in relation to the suggestion that there be a new minister and, presumably, a new minister for the purpose of changing a very unsatisfactory condition which does now exist. Any suggestion that the situation is satisfactory now is simply a denial of all the facts which have been placed before us, and a denial of the known facts in the possession of every member of this house.
We have had assurance after assurance that everything was being done that should be done and then, when an opportunity is presented to obtain the facts, we get the clear and unchallengeable evidence that a great deal does remain to be done. The suggestion was made that the bill go back for reconsideration. That has been disposed of. Now we are in committee, and this is the point at which an amendment may be moved calling for the appointment of an associate minister of national defence for air. In view of the fact that the government has not seen fit to reconsider the measure it will not be possible to define by amendment in a satisfactory way the duties that should be exercised. Nevertheless, if an amendment were accepted which simply called for the appointment of an associate minister of national defence for air, that term in itself would be sufficiently descriptive to indicate the nature of the duties which could be defined for that minister under the section now before us.
The proposal has been made that we should, in this case, follow the practice which has
[The Chairman.]
been adopted in other countries of the commonwealth as well as in the United States. Every one of us recognizes that the procedure is different in the United States. Every one of us recognizes that they do not carry on government under the parliamentary system. Nevertheless, from the point of view of administration, it is significant that they have chosen to deal with this extremely important part of the responsibility of government in the very way we are suggesting it should be dealt with here. The difference between their system and our parliamentary system does not in itself render inapplicable the reasons they have adopted that course. Since it is so generally agreed that we depend very largely on the efficiency of their effort for the combined strength of the western nations, I think most of us will hope that their system is efficient. Most of us do believe that the present President of the United States has had that measure of military experience which would give him a very unusual appreciation of the type of administrative organization that would be most effective under circumstances of this kind.
The proposal that there be an associate minister of national defence for air does not create any difficulties from the point of view of administration. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made this clear. He has indicated that no problems arose when an associate minister was appointed before. He has made it clear that at a time when, in addition to an associate minister, there were ministers of defence for air and naval services, no problems arose as to overlapping jurisdiction or competitive efforts to advance the cause of one service or the other.
One of the reasons it does seem particularly appropriate that we should have an associate minister of defence for air is that this country, more than any other country in the world, has demonstrated its special qualifications in the air. This country, more than any other country in the world, has demonstrated the aptitude of our young men for this still comparatively new branch of the service. Moreover our geographical position makes it essential that we develop our air service in a way that will make it easy for us to contribute that form of defence which could be most effective.
Since this matter was discussed this afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I have heard certain comments made over the radio that emphasized that a minister for air services would mean added national defence costs. Actually what might well happen, and what we believe would happen, is that there could be substantially reduced national defence costs and


substantially reduced taxes as a result of that, with still greater effectiveness and hitting power if we rationalized our whole defence organization with appreciation of the fact that Canada occupies a peculiarly favoured position from the point of view of developing air defence. By the employment of air transport, by the employment of long-range aircraft of every type, we could develop a mobile force with armoured forces which could be moved rapidly to any point either in our own country or outside, with the highest economy that could be established. In this modern world, with the material resources and human skills we possess, we should be concentrating every effort to give every man in a unit the greatest hitting power that our industrial skill makes possible.
The way to do that is to develop fast, mobile forces which can be moved by air to any part of the world. This proposal has already been made on a number of occasions from this side of the house. The appointment of an associate minister of defence for air would not only make it possible to emphasize the development of our air service, but also to co-ordinate the development of our air services with the development of other forces. It would increase the hitting power per man, and in that way achieve great economy of force and great economy of manpower.
The time for a re-examination of our defence organization is long overdue. One of the ways to achieve it is to appoint a minister particularly responsible for the administration of that part of our defence organization which will be called upon to spend more than half of every tax dollar raised for the purposes of national defence. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes):
